# Wi-Fi Station Mode & Data Upload {.unnumbered}

With our power management optimized and our ESP32 reliably waking up from deep sleep, it's time to give our weather station a voice! In this chapter, we will introduce Wi-Fi capabilities to the ESP32.

Instead of just saving the data to the local SD card, the ESP32 will now connect to a local Wi-Fi network and upload the sensor readings to a server using an HTTP POST request.

## The Code

> **Ready-to-use project:** The complete code for this firmware is available in the repository here: [`06_wifi_station`](https://github.com/wg1d/personal-autonomous-weather-station/tree/main/firmware/Phase-03/06_wifi_station)

> **Further Reading:** For a deeper dive into Wi-Fi connectivity on the ESP32, you can refer to this excellent [uPesy tutorial on connecting an ESP32 to Wi-Fi](https://www.upesy.fr/blogs/tutorials/how-to-connect-wifi-acces-point-with-esp32).

### Code Cleanup Notice
As our firmware grows more advanced, the `setup()` function is becoming quite long. For this step, the code is structurally identical to Phase 02. We have simply inserted the new Wi-Fi logic right after the SD card write operation. In **Phase 04**, we will perform a massive architectural refactoring to split this monolithic code into clean `.cpp` and `.h` files!

### Connecting to a Network
To connect the ESP32 to the internet (or your local network), it needs to act as a **Wi-Fi Station**. Just like your smartphone or laptop, the ESP32 must know two pieces of information to connect to your router:

1. **SSID** (The name of the Wi-Fi network)
2. **Password**

### Securing Credentials with `secrets.h`
Hardcoding Wi-Fi passwords directly into your main code is a massive security risk, especially if you plan to share your code or upload it to GitHub. 

To solve this, we create a template file called `secrets.example.h` inside our project folder:

```cpp
#ifndef SECRETS_H
#define SECRETS_H

// IMPORTANT: Do NOT commit your actual credentials to GitHub!
// 1. Rename this file to 'secrets.h' (which is ignored by Git)
// 2. Replace the placeholders below with your actual Wi-Fi credentials

const char* WIFI_SSID = "YOUR_WIFI_SSID";
const char* WIFI_PASSWORD = "YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD";

#endif
```

We then add `secrets.h` to our `.gitignore` file. Anyone who clones the project simply renames the template to `secrets.h` and adds their credentials. This guarantees that your passwords stay safely on your local computer and never get uploaded to the internet.

### The Target Server
Before we can upload data, the ESP32 needs to know *where* to send it. At the top of your `.ino` file (right below the `WAKEUP_INTERVAL_SECONDS`), we define the IP address of our local computer which will soon host our dummy backend server:

```cpp
// Dummy server endpoint (Update with your computer's local IP address)
const char* serverName = "http://192.168.1.100:5000/upload";
```

> **Check your IP Address!** Make sure to replace `192.168.1.100` with your actual local network IP address, otherwise the ESP32 will fail to connect (Error `-1`).
> 
> **How to find your IP address:**
> - **Windows:** Open Command Prompt and type `ipconfig` (look for "IPv4 Address").
> - **macOS:** Open Terminal and type `ipconfig getifaddr en0`.
> - **Linux:** Open Terminal and type `hostname -I`.

### The Wi-Fi Upload Logic

In our main firmware, we `#include "secrets.h"` and add the upload logic right after saving to the SD card. 

Here is how the ESP32 handles the connection:

```cpp
  // 4. Upload Data via Wi-Fi
  WiFi.begin(WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD);
  Serial.print("Connecting to WiFi...");
  
  // Timeout after 10 seconds to save battery if network is down
  int wifi_timeout = 0;
  while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED && wifi_timeout < 20) {
    delay(500);
    Serial.print(".");
    wifi_timeout++;
  }

  if(WiFi.status() == WL_CONNECTED) {
    Serial.println("\nConnected to WiFi network");
    HTTPClient http;
    http.begin(serverName); // Dummy server endpoint
    http.addHeader("Content-Type", "text/csv");
    
    // Open the CSV file from the SD card
    File file = SD.open("/weather_data.csv");
    if (file) {
      Serial.print("Uploading CSV file to server: ");
      Serial.println(serverName);
      
      // Stream the file directly to the server to save RAM
      int httpResponseCode = http.sendRequest("POST", &file, file.size());
      
      if (httpResponseCode > 0) {
        Serial.printf("HTTP Response code: %d\n", httpResponseCode);
      } else {
        Serial.printf("Error code: %d\n", httpResponseCode);
      }
      file.close();
    } else {
      Serial.println("Failed to open CSV file for uploading.");
    }
    http.end();
  } else {
    Serial.println("\nWiFi connection failed, skipped upload");
  }

  // Turn off Wi-Fi to save power before sleeping
  WiFi.disconnect(true);
  WiFi.mode(WIFI_OFF);
  
  // Power OFF the SD card module now that the upload is complete
  SD.end();
  digitalWrite(SD_OFF_PIN, LOW);
```

## How It Works

1.  **Timeouts Save Batteries:** The most battery-intensive action an ESP32 can perform is searching for a Wi-Fi network. If your router goes offline, a standard `while(WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED)` loop will get permanently stuck, draining the battery in hours. We implement a hard 10-second timeout. If the network isn't found, we abort the upload and go back to sleep.
2.  **Robust Offline Capabilities (CSV Streaming):** Instead of uploading a single `JSON` payload representing the live reading, we stream the *entire* `weather_data.csv` file from the SD card directly into the HTTP POST request. Why? Because if the Wi-Fi goes down for 3 days, the ESP32 will continue saving data to the SD card offline. The instant the Wi-Fi comes back online, it uploads the complete CSV file, meaning the server automatically receives all the missed offline data without writing complex queuing algorithms!
    
> **Future Optimization:** You might be wondering: *"If this station runs for a year, won't uploading a massive CSV file every 30 seconds drain the battery?"* Yes, it will! For now, we are keeping the architecture simple to focus purely on Wi-Fi connectivity. We will dedicate an entire future chapter to "Log Rotation and Smart Queuing" to solve this exact problem elegantly!

3.  **Radio Shutdown:** Before calling `esp_deep_sleep_start()`, we explicitly call `WiFi.disconnect(true)` and `WiFi.mode(WIFI_OFF)`. This ensures the Wi-Fi radio is cleanly shut down, preventing any microscopic current leaks while the chip sleeps.

## Next Steps

Now that our ESP32 is screaming data into the void, we need something to listen to it! In the next chapter, we will build a dummy backend server to receive these POST requests.
